C(−1.0) on dev_a1 gives +0.39 ± 1.88 (12 wrong→right, 11 right→wrong), against −1.56 for C(−1.5) on the same problems. The original's answers are identical to pass 39 (21.9%, 70 cut), so the two doses can be compared directly. The lower dose frees fewer loops (cut-offs 21.1% against 14.1%) and causes fewer losses (11 against 15). That matches the trade-off the flip proxy predicted, but the difference lies well within noise.

To reach the +1.9 pooled DEV bar, the remaining three DEV sets would need to average about +2.4, which is unlikely. I'm adding a futility stop now, before seeing more data: after dev_a2, if pooled DEV for C(−1.0) is below +0.8, I stop the C(−1.0) line and keep the remaining passes. Next is dev_a2, where C(−1.5) gave −1.17.

The notes are updated, and C(−1.0) is unchanged (14 tensors). This pass measures it on dev_a2, where C(−1.5) gave −1.17 (9/12) with cut-offs at 14.8%. Under the futility rule set beforehand, pooled DEV over dev_a1 and dev_a2 below +0.8 ends the C(−1.0) line. At or above +0.8, I'll continue to dev_b1 and dev_b2.

C(−1.0) on dev_a2 gives +1.17 ± 1.61 (10/7), with cut-offs at 18.4%. Pooled over dev_a it is +0.78 (22 wrong→right, 18 right→wrong over 512), just below the +0.8 futility threshold I set before this pass, so the C(−1.0) line stops. Even with perfect follow-up, the original +1.9 DEV bar would require about +3.0 on each of dev_b1 and dev_b2, far above anything any C variant has produced there.

The two doses do behave as the flip proxy predicted. C(−1.0) frees fewer loops (cut-offs 21% and 18%, against 14% and 15% for C(−1.5)) and causes fewer losses on finished answers. On dev_a it scores about 2 points above C(−1.5), but that is unpaired between doses, measured on the set used to build the direction, and within noise. I'm restoring the frozen submission C(−1.5) from /work/best_final and verifying it byte for byte.

The submission C(−1.5) is restored and verified. Six passes remain, which is not enough to build and fully validate a new edit, so any further work should explain the edit's one known weakness. That weakness is the net loss on problems the original finished: 70 wrong→right against 97 right→wrong. This analysis uses no pass. I'll take the right→wrong cases among originally finished problems across all C(−1.5) generation passes (13, 28, 29–33, 39, 40). Each lost answer is sorted three ways: the edit made it loop (now cut), it ended with a different wrong number, or it changed solution style. Style is judged by the first token, "Let" (plain) against "Here" (markdown), which I earlier found tied to accuracy. If many losses are newly cut answers, C also creates loops in some problems. If most are style changes, the collateral damage acts through the style-switch effect seen earlier. Either finding is useful in the report, even without a pass left to act on it.
